tldr: Attard works through a checklist for production Java containers: pinned and layered images, jlink runtimes on slim or scratch bases, AOT cache, compact object headers, memory flags, lifecycle and hardening.
summary: Attard, from Oracle's Java team, starts with the environment variables the JVM reads. _JAVA_OPTIONS overrides the command line, JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS is where VM flags belong so one image can run with different settings, and agents need JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS because it is read earlier. Tags such as jdk:25 on the Oracle Container Registry are mutable, so he pins images by digest. Using Dive, he compares a Spring Boot fat JAR, one 56 MB layer, with the extracted Spring layers, where dependencies take 56 MB and the application an 18 KB final layer, so a code change rebuilds and ships only that.

Next he trims the runtime. jlink builds a runtime with only the needed modules; keep jdk.jcmd and jdk.jfr for diagnostics. The OS layer drops from about 100 MB on Oracle Linux slim to 28 MB distroless and about 6 MB on a scratch image holding only Java's native libraries, which he frames as less attack surface. Multi-arch base images give AMD64 and ARM64 builds. The JDK 25 AOT cache gave the biggest startup gain on an unchanged JAR. Because it depends on classpath order, he writes a sorted classpath into an argument file during the training run and reuses that file at runtime.

Compact object headers (8 instead of 12 bytes, opt-in in JDK 25 and, he said, default in 27) slightly raised throughput, cut latency from 15 to 14 ms and reduced GC runs. In a 1 GB container Java defaults to the Serial GC and a 25% heap, so he sets MaxRAMPercentage=75. He separates OutOfMemoryError from the kernel OOM-killing PID 1, showing that a 256 MB heap in a 256 MB container starts and only dies under load unless AlwaysPreTouch is set. He finishes with ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, heap dumps to a volume, graceful shutdown with readiness probes, and non-root, read-only, capability-dropped containers.
keyPoints: Use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS for VM flags so one image can be run and benchmarked with different settings; agents must go in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS; JAVA_OPTS is not read by the JVM at all.
Pin base images by digest, because tags such as jdk:25 move with every update.
Layered Spring Boot images put the 56 MB of dependencies and the 18 KB application in separate layers, so code changes rebuild and transfer only the small one.

A jlink runtime on a scratch image with hand-copied native libraries brings the OS layer to about 6 MB, against 100 MB for Oracle Linux slim and 28 MB for distroless; keep jdk.jcmd and jdk.jfr for diagnostics.
The JDK 25 AOT cache is tied to classpath order; generate and run from the same sorted argument file, and decide whether AOTMode=on (fail if the cache is unusable) is right for production.
Without flags, a 1 GB container gets the Serial GC and a 25% max heap; MaxRAMPercentage=75 makes the heap scale with container memory.
OutOfMemoryError and the container OOM killer are different failures; AlwaysPreTouch exposes an oversized heap at startup instead of under load.
Recommended flags: ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and HeapDumpPath pointing at a persistent volume.
takeaways: Check whether your containers set a heap size; if not, add -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (Attard uses 75) through JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS.
Split your Spring Boot image into dependency and application layers and confirm the result with Dive.
Build a jlink runtime for one service, including jdk.jcmd and jdk.jfr, and run it as a non-root user on a read-only filesystem.
Try the JDK 25 AOT cache and compact object headers, measuring startup, throughput and GC against a baseline first.
Add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError and heap dumps to a mounted path, and remove any flag that measurement shows does nothing.

quotes.text: The issue is not size, but it is reducing attack surface area.
If you added a flag which is not giving you anything, it's better to remove it.

watchIf: You package Java services as containers and want a practical list of image, JVM flag and hardening settings, each backed by a measurement.
